modules.title: Algebras, duals and representations on a conjugate module
modules.doc:
The conjugate module of an algebra, the conjugate dual, and the conjugate of a representation.

## i. Overview

`Physlib.Mathematics.Modules.ConjModule` carries `ConjModule M`, the module `M` with scalars
acting through `star`, together with the conjugate-linear equivalence `conjEquiv`. This module
extends that in three directions, all of which a conjugate Weyl field needs.

First, when the module is a ring the conjugate module is a ring too, and the conjugate module
of a `k`-algebra is a `k`-algebra: the same multiplication, with scalars acting through `star`.

Second, the dual of `M` and the dual of `ConjModule M` are conjugate-linearly equivalent, by
`conjDualEquiv`, so a linear functional on a field has a conjugate functional on the conjugate
field.

Third, a representation `ρ` of `G` on `M` has a conjugate representation `ρ.conj` of `G` on
`ConjModule M`, given by the same maps `ρ g` read through `conjEquiv`. Conjugation commutes
with the constructions representations are built from: it is involutive, it passes through
products and `Pi` types, and over `ℂ` it turns a complex-linear endomorphism into its
conjugate.

## ii. Key results

- `ConjModule.instAlgebra` : the conjugate module of a `k`-algebra is a `k`-algebra.
- `ConjModule.conjDualEquiv` : the dual of `M` and the dual of `ConjModule M` are
  conjugate-linearly equivalent.
- `Representation.conj` : the conjugate of a representation.
- `ConjModule.prodEquiv`, `ConjModule.piEquiv` : conjugation commutes with products.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. The conjugate module of an algebra
- B. The conjugate dual
- C. The conjugate of a representation
- D. Functoriality, and conjugation of tensor products
- E. Endomorphisms of the conjugate module

## iv. References

The conjugate module itself is in `Physlib.Mathematics.Modules.ConjModule`.

sections.text: ## A. The conjugate module of an algebra
## C. The conjugate of a representation

## D. Functoriality, and conjugation of tensor products

Conjugation is monoidal: `ConjModule M ⊗ ConjModule N ≃ ConjModule (M ⊗ N)`, the identity
on pure tensors. The map is honestly `k`-linear because the twist on each factor cancels
against the twist on the target.

Everything below routes through `conjEquiv` rather than relying on definitional unfolding
of the `ConjModule` synonym. Writing `m ⊗ₜ n` for `m : ConjModule M` makes elaboration
pick the *twisted* module instances, landing in the wrong tensor product; converting
explicitly with `conjEquiv` fixes every instance by construction.

## E. Endomorphisms of the conjugate module

An endomorphism of `M` is read on `ConjModule M` through `conjEquiv`. Conjugating twists
nothing at the level of the additive group, so the structural identities hold
definitionally; only the real-scalar one needs an argument.

declarations.name: Representation.conj_trivial_apply
declarations.doc: The conjugate of the trivial representation acts trivially.
declarations.statement:
lemma _root_.Representation.conj_trivial_apply {G : Type*} [Group G] (g : G)
    (m : ConjModule M) : (Representation.trivial k G M).conj g m = m

declarations.name: Representation.conj_trivial_dual_apply
declarations.doc: The dual of the conjugate of the trivial representation acts trivially.
declarations.statement:
lemma _root_.Representation.conj_trivial_dual_apply {G : Type*} [Group G] (g : G)
    (φ : Module.Dual k (ConjModule M)) :
    ((Representation.trivial k G M).conj).dual g φ = φ

declarations.name: ConjModule.map
declarations.doc:
Functoriality of conjugation: a `k`-linear map induces a `k`-linear map of the
conjugate modules, given by the same underlying function.
declarations.statement: def map (f : M →ₗ[k] N) : ConjModule M →ₗ[k] ConjModule N

declarations.name: ConjModule.map_apply
declarations.statement: lemma map_apply (f : M →ₗ[k] N) (x : ConjModule M) : map f x = f x

declarations.name: ConjModule.prodEquiv
declarations.doc:
**Conjugation commutes with finite products.** The conjugate of a product is the product
of the conjugates, by the identity underlying function: the twisted scalar action is applied
componentwise.
declarations.statement: def prodEquiv : ConjModule (M × N) ≃ₗ[k] ConjModule M × ConjModule N

declarations.name: ConjModule.prodEquiv_apply
declarations.statement:
lemma prodEquiv_apply (x : ConjModule (M × N)) :
    prodEquiv (k := k) x = (map (LinearMap.fst k M N) x, map (LinearMap.snd k M N) x)

declarations.name: ConjModule.piEquiv
declarations.doc:
**Conjugation commutes with arbitrary products.** The conjugate of a product of a
family of modules is the product of their conjugates, by the identity underlying
function: the twisted scalar action is applied componentwise, so no finiteness of the
index type is needed.
declarations.statement: def piEquiv : ConjModule (∀ i, P i) ≃ₗ[k] ∀ i, ConjModule (P i)

declarations.name: ConjModule.piEquiv_apply
declarations.statement:
lemma piEquiv_apply (x : ConjModule (∀ i, P i)) (i : ι) :
    (piEquiv P : ConjModule (∀ i, P i) ≃ₗ[k] ∀ i, ConjModule (P i)) x i
      = map (k := k) (LinearMap.proj i) x

declarations.name: ConjModule.piEquiv_symm_apply
declarations.statement:
lemma piEquiv_symm_apply (x : ∀ i, ConjModule (P i)) (i : ι) :
    map (k := k) (LinearMap.proj i)
        ((piEquiv P : ConjModule (∀ i, P i) ≃ₗ[k] ∀ i, ConjModule (P i)).symm x) = x i

declarations.name: ConjModule.instFinite
declarations.doc:
The conjugate module of a finite free module is finite: the conjugated basis
`Basis.conj` is indexed by the same type.
declarations.statement:
instance instFinite [Module.Free k M] [Module.Finite k M] :
    Module.Finite k (ConjModule M)

declarations.name: ConjModule.tensorHom
declarations.doc:
The canonical `k`-linear map `ConjModule M ⊗ ConjModule N → ConjModule (M ⊗ N)`,
the identity on pure tensors.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def tensorHom : ConjModule M ⊗[k] ConjModule N →ₗ[k] ConjModule (M ⊗[k] N)

declarations.name: ConjModule.tensorHom_tmul
declarations.statement:
lemma tensorHom_tmul (m : ConjModule M) (n : ConjModule N) :
    tensorHom (k := k) (m ⊗ₜ[k] n)
      = conjEquiv (k := k) (M := M ⊗[k] N)
        ((conjEquiv (k := k) (M := M)).symm m ⊗ₜ[k] (conjEquiv (k := k) (M := N)).symm n)

declarations.name: ConjModule.tensorInv
declarations.doc:
The inverse map `ConjModule (M ⊗ N) → ConjModule M ⊗ ConjModule N`, again the identity
on pure tensors. A `k`-linear map out of `ConjModule X` is the same data as a `k`-linear
map into `ConjModule` of the target, which is what `map` and `involution` package here.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def tensorInv : ConjModule (M ⊗[k] N) →ₗ[k] ConjModule M ⊗[k] ConjModule N

declarations.name: ConjModule.tensorEquiv
declarations.statement:
noncomputable def tensorEquiv :
    ConjModule M ⊗[k] ConjModule N ≃ₗ[k] ConjModule (M ⊗[k] N)

declarations.name: ConjModule.tensorEquiv_tmul
declarations.statement:
lemma tensorEquiv_tmul (m : ConjModule M) (n : ConjModule N) :
    tensorEquiv (k := k) (m ⊗ₜ[k] n)
      = conjEquiv (k := k) (M := M ⊗[k] N)
        ((conjEquiv (k := k) (M := M)).symm m ⊗ₜ[k] (conjEquiv (k := k) (M := N)).symm n)

declarations.name: ConjModule.tensorEquiv_symm_conjEquiv_tmul
declarations.statement:
lemma tensorEquiv_symm_conjEquiv_tmul (m : M) (n : N) :
    (tensorEquiv (k := k) (M := M) (N := N)).symm
        (conjEquiv (k := k) (M := M ⊗[k] N) (m ⊗ₜ[k] n))
      = conjEquiv (k := k) (M := M) m ⊗ₜ[k] conjEquiv (k := k) (M := N) n

declarations.name: ConjModule.endConj
declarations.doc:
A linear endomorphism read on the conjugate module: the same underlying map,
through the identity `conjEquiv`. Conjugating twists nothing at the level of the
additive group, so all structural identities (`comp`, `add`, `neg`, sums) hold
definitionally.

declarations.name: ConjModule.endConj_apply
declarations.statement:
lemma endConj_apply {k : Type*} [CommRing k] [StarRing k] {M : Type*}
    [AddCommGroup M] [Module k M] (f : M →ₗ[k] M) (v : ConjModule M) :
    ConjModule.endConj f v =
      conjEquiv (k := k) (M := M) (f ((conjEquiv (k := k) (M := M)).symm v))

declarations.name: ConjModule.endConj_id
ConjModule.endConj_comp
ConjModule.endConj_add
ConjModule.endConj_neg
ConjModule.endConj_multiset_sum
declarations.statement:
lemma endConj_multiset_sum {k : Type*} [CommRing k] [StarRing k]
    {M : Type*} [AddCommGroup M] [Module k M] (S : Multiset (M →ₗ[k] M)) :
    ConjModule.endConj S.sum = (S.map ConjModule.endConj).sum

declarations.name: ConjModule.endConj_real_smul
declarations.doc:
Conjugation of endomorphisms commutes with real scalars: the star on the
conjugated complex scalar is invisible on the reals.
declarations.statement:
lemma endConj_real_smul {M : Type*} [AddCommGroup M] [Module ℂ M]
    (r : ℝ) (f : M →ₗ[ℂ] M) :
    ConjModule.endConj (r • f) = r • ConjModule.endConj f

modules.title: Sums over the antidiagonal of a multiset
modules.doc:
## i. Overview

Combinatorial identities for sums indexed by `Multiset.antidiagonal`: associativity and
exchange of nested antidiagonal sums, collapsing a sum whose terms vanish off one slot, and
the interaction with linear maps and tensor products. These are the bookkeeping behind the
all-orders Leibniz rules of the jet calculus.

## ii. Key results

- `sum_antidiagonal_assoc` : coassociativity of antidiagonal sums: summing over `s = u + v` and then
  `u = x + y` is summing over `s = x + t` and then `t = y + v`
- `sum_antidiagonal_exchange`
- `sum_linearMap_apply` : a multiset sum of linear maps, applied: the sum of the applications
- `tmul_sum` : a pure tensor against a multiset sum distributes over the sum

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Sums over the antidiagonal

## iv. References

* None.

declarations.name: Multiset.sum_antidiagonal_assoc
declarations.doc:
Coassociativity of antidiagonal sums: summing over `s = u + v` and then `u = x + y`
is summing over `s = x + t` and then `t = y + v`.
declarations.statement:
lemma sum_antidiagonal_assoc {ι M : Type*} [AddCommMonoid M]
    (s : Multiset ι) (h : Multiset ι → Multiset ι → Multiset ι → M) :
    (s.antidiagonal.map fun p =>
      (p.1.antidiagonal.map fun q => h q.1 q.2 p.2).sum).sum =
    (s.antidiagonal.map fun p =>
      (p.2.antidiagonal.map fun q => h p.1 q.1 q.2).sum).sum

declarations.name: Multiset.sum_antidiagonal_exchange
declarations.doc:
The exchange law of doubly-split antidiagonal sums: splitting `s = u + v` and then
`u = x + y`, `v = z + w` is, with the middle parts exchanged, splitting `s = u' + v'`
and then `u' = x + z`, `v' = y + w`.
declarations.statement:
lemma sum_antidiagonal_exchange {ι M : Type*} [AddCommMonoid M]
    (s : Multiset ι) (h : Multiset ι → Multiset ι → Multiset ι → Multiset ι → M) :
    (s.antidiagonal.map fun p =>
      (p.1.antidiagonal.map fun q =>
        (p.2.antidiagonal.map fun r => h q.1 q.2 r.1 r.2).sum).sum).sum =
    (s.antidiagonal.map fun p =>
      (p.1.antidiagonal.map fun q =>
        (p.2.antidiagonal.map fun r => h q.1 r.1 q.2 r.2).sum).sum).sum

declarations.name: Multiset.sum_linearMap_apply
declarations.doc: A multiset sum of linear maps, applied: the sum of the applications.
declarations.statement:
lemma sum_linearMap_apply {R M N : Type*} [Semiring R] [AddCommMonoid M]
    [AddCommMonoid N] [Module R M] [Module R N] (S : Multiset (M →ₗ[R] N)) (x : M) :
    S.sum x = (S.map fun f => f x).sum

declarations.name: Multiset.tmul_sum
declarations.doc: A pure tensor against a multiset sum distributes over the sum.
declarations.statement:
lemma tmul_sum {R M N : Type*} [CommSemiring R] [AddCommMonoid M]
    [AddCommMonoid N] [Module R M] [Module R N] (m : M) (S : Multiset N) :
    m ⊗ₜ[R] S.sum = (S.map fun n => m ⊗ₜ[R] n).sum

declarations.name: Multiset.sum_antidiagonal_swap
declarations.doc: Antidiagonal sums are symmetric under swapping the two parts.
declarations.statement:
lemma sum_antidiagonal_swap {ι M : Type*} [AddCommMonoid M]
    (s : Multiset ι) (h : Multiset ι → Multiset ι → M) :
    (s.antidiagonal.map fun p => h p.1 p.2).sum =
    (s.antidiagonal.map fun p => h p.2 p.1).sum

declarations.name: Multiset.sum_map_neg''
declarations.doc: A multiset sum of negations is the negation of the sum.
declarations.statement:
lemma sum_map_neg'' {ι M : Type*} [AddCommGroup M]
    (s : Multiset ι) (f : ι → M) :
    (s.map fun i => -f i).sum = -(s.map f).sum

declarations.name: Multiset.sum_map_finsetSum
declarations.doc: The exchange of a finite sum with a multiset sum.
declarations.statement:
lemma sum_map_finsetSum {α β M : Type*} [AddCommMonoid M]
    (m : Multiset α) (t : Finset β) (f : β → α → M) :
    (m.map fun a => ∑ b ∈ t, f b a).sum = ∑ b ∈ t, (m.map (f b)).sum

declarations.name: Multiset.fst_le_of_mem_antidiagonal
declarations.doc: The first part of a splitting of `s` is a sub-multiset of `s`.
declarations.statement:
lemma fst_le_of_mem_antidiagonal {ι : Type*} {s : Multiset ι} {p : Multiset ι × Multiset ι}
    (hp : p ∈ s.antidiagonal) : p.1 ≤ s

declarations.name: Multiset.snd_le_of_mem_antidiagonal
declarations.doc: The second part of a splitting of `s` is a sub-multiset of `s`.
declarations.statement:
lemma snd_le_of_mem_antidiagonal {ι : Type*} {s : Multiset ι} {p : Multiset ι × Multiset ι}
    (hp : p ∈ s.antidiagonal) : p.2 ≤ s

declarations.name: Multiset.sum_antidiagonal_eq_of_fst_ne_zero
declarations.doc:
A sum over the antidiagonal of a family vanishing off `p.1 = 0` collapses to the
single term at `(0, s)`.
declarations.statement:
lemma sum_antidiagonal_eq_of_fst_ne_zero {ι M : Type*} [AddCommMonoid M]
    (s : Multiset ι) (F : Multiset ι × Multiset ι → M)
    (hF : ∀ p ∈ s.antidiagonal, p.1 ≠ 0 → F p = 0) :
    (s.antidiagonal.map F).sum = F (0, s)

declarations.name: Multiset.sum_antidiagonal_eq_of_snd_ne_zero
declarations.doc:
A sum over the antidiagonal of a family vanishing off `p.2 = 0` collapses to the
single term at `(s, 0)`.
declarations.statement:
lemma sum_antidiagonal_eq_of_snd_ne_zero {ι M : Type*} [AddCommMonoid M]
    (s : Multiset ι) (F : Multiset ι × Multiset ι → M)
    (hF : ∀ p ∈ s.antidiagonal, p.2 ≠ 0 → F p = 0) :
    (s.antidiagonal.map F).sum = F (s, 0)

declarations.name: Multiset.sum_antidiagonal_middle_exchange
declarations.doc: The exchange of the second and third slot in a nested antidiagonal sum.
declarations.statement:
lemma sum_antidiagonal_middle_exchange {ι M : Type*} [AddCommMonoid M]
    (s : Multiset ι) (h : Multiset ι → Multiset ι → Multiset ι → M) :
    (s.antidiagonal.map fun p =>
        (p.1.antidiagonal.map fun q => h q.1 q.2 p.2).sum).sum
      = (s.antidiagonal.map fun p =>
        (p.1.antidiagonal.map fun q => h q.1 p.2 q.2).sum).sum

modules.title: Polynomials invariant under fiberwise translations of variables
modules.doc:
## i. Overview

Let `π` be an idempotent map on the index type of a multivariate polynomial ring
over an infinite integral domain, thought of as assigning to each variable a
canonical representative of its fiber. A polynomial that is invariant under
simultaneously translating, for each fiber, all the variables in that fiber by a
common constant is a polynomial in the differences `X i - X (π i)`.

This is the algebraic heart of the statement that the gauge-invariant elements of
the jet algebra of an abelian gauge boson are generated by the derivatives of the
field strength: the Maurer–Cartan shift translates all jet coordinates with the
same symmetrized multi-index by a common amount, and the differences of such
coordinates are the derivatives of the field strength.

## ii. Key results

- `eval_aeval` : evaluation of a substitution of a multivariate polynomial: substitution followed by
  evaluation is evaluation at the evaluated substituents
- `aeval_update_zero_eq_of_forall_aeval_add_eq` : a polynomial invariant under all translations of a
  fixed variable is unchanged by setting that variable to zero
- `notMem_vars_of_forall_aeval_add_eq` : a polynomial invariant under all translations of a fixed
  variable does not involve that variable
- `mem_adjoin_range_X_sub_X_of_forall_aeval_add_eq` : a multivariate polynomial over an infinite
  integral domain that is invariant under simultaneously translating, for every fiber of an
  idempotent map `π` on the variables, all the variables in that fiber by a common constant, is a
  polynomial in the differences `X i - X (π i)`

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Invariance under fiberwise translations

## iv. References

* None.

declarations.name: MvPolynomial.eval_aeval
declarations.doc:
Evaluation of a substitution of a multivariate polynomial: substitution followed
by evaluation is evaluation at the evaluated substituents.
declarations.statement:
lemma eval_aeval (x : I → R) (g : I → MvPolynomial I R) (p : MvPolynomial I R) :
    eval x (aeval g p) = eval (fun i => eval x (g i)) p

declarations.name: MvPolynomial.aeval_update_zero_eq_of_forall_aeval_add_eq
declarations.doc:
A polynomial invariant under all translations of a fixed variable is unchanged
by setting that variable to zero.
declarations.statement:
lemma aeval_update_zero_eq_of_forall_aeval_add_eq (Q : MvPolynomial I R) (j : I)
    (hQ : ∀ r : R, aeval (fun i => X i + C (if i = j then r else 0)) Q = Q) :
    aeval (fun i => if i = j then 0 else X i) Q = Q

declarations.name: MvPolynomial.notMem_vars_of_forall_aeval_add_eq
declarations.doc:
A polynomial invariant under all translations of a fixed variable does not
involve that variable.
declarations.statement:
lemma notMem_vars_of_forall_aeval_add_eq (Q : MvPolynomial I R) (j : I)
    (hQ : ∀ r : R, aeval (fun i => X i + C (if i = j then r else 0)) Q = Q) :
    j ∉ Q.vars

declarations.name: MvPolynomial.mem_adjoin_range_X_sub_X_of_forall_aeval_add_eq
declarations.doc:
A multivariate polynomial over an infinite integral domain that is invariant
under simultaneously translating, for every fiber of an idempotent map `π` on the
variables, all the variables in that fiber by a common constant, is a polynomial
in the differences `X i - X (π i)`.
declarations.statement:
lemma mem_adjoin_range_X_sub_X_of_forall_aeval_add_eq (π : I → I)
    (hπ : ∀ i, π (π i) = π i) (P : MvPolynomial I R)
    (hP : ∀ (i₀ : I) (r : R),
      aeval (fun i => X i + C (if π i = π i₀ then r else 0)) P = P) :
    P ∈ Algebra.adjoin R (Set.range fun i => (X i - X (π i) : MvPolynomial I R))

modules.title: Causal support geometry
modules.doc:
## i. Overview

Causal futures and pasts describe the allowed support of linear field responses.

## ii. Key results

- `reverse` : Reversing the causal direction exchanges retarded and advanced support.
- `reverse` : Reversing the causal direction exchanges retarded and advanced support.
- `causalFuture` : The events reachable from at least one event of a source set.
- `causalPast` : The events able to influence at least one event of a target set.
- `causalHull` : The union of the causal past and future of a set.
- `IsSpacelikeCompact` : A closed field support is spacelike compact when it lies in the causal hull
  of a compact set.
- `HasCompactCausalDiamonds` : Compact causal diamonds are the geometric compactness input for Green
  exactness.
- `causalFuture` : The events reachable from at least one event of a source set.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Causal support geometry
- B. Past-compact and future-compact support

## iv. References

None.

## A. Causal support geometry

- `reverse` : Reversing the causal direction exchanges retarded and advanced support.
- `reverse` : Reversing the causal direction exchanges retarded and advanced support.
- `causalFuture` : The events reachable from at least one event of a source set.
- `causalPast` : The events able to influence at least one event of a target set.
- `causalHull` : The union of the causal past and future of a set.
- `IsSpacelikeCompact` : A closed field support is spacelike compact when it lies in the causal hull
  of a compact set.
- `HasCompactCausalDiamonds` : Compact causal diamonds are the geometric compactness input for Green
  exactness.

Lemmas: `subset_causalFuture`, `subset_causalPast`, `causalFuture_mono`, `causalPast_mono`,
`causalHull_mono`, `causalFuture_empty`, `causalPast_empty`, `causalFuture_union`,
`causalPast_union`, `causalFuture_idem` and more.

## B. Past-compact and future-compact support

- `causalFuture` : The events reachable from at least one event of a source set.
- `IsPastCompact` : A set is past compact when its intersection with the causal past of every
  compact set is compact.

Lemmas: `mono`, `isPastCompact_empty`, `union`, `causalFuture_inter_causalPast`,
`isPastCompact_of_futureSupported`, `isClosed_causalFuture`.

declarations.name: CausalRelation
declarations.doc:
The causal relation used to bound field propagation. Further geometric hypotheses belong
in the results requiring them rather than in this minimal structure.
declarations.statement:
structure CausalRelation (M : Type*) where
  /-- An event can influence a causally later event. -/
  Precedes : M → M → Prop
  /-- Every event lies in its own causal future. -/
  refl : ∀ p, Precedes p p
  /-- Successive causal propagation is causal. -/
  trans : ∀ {p q r}, Precedes p q → Precedes q r → Precedes p r

declarations.name: CausalRelation.reverse
declarations.doc: Reversing the causal direction exchanges retarded and advanced support.
declarations.statement: def reverse : CausalRelation M

declarations.name: CausalRelation.causalFuture
declarations.doc: The events reachable from at least one event of a source set.
declarations.statement: def causalFuture (A : Set M) : Set M

declarations.name: CausalRelation.causalPast

declarations.statement: def causalPast (A : Set M) : Set M

declarations.name: CausalRelation.causalHull
declarations.doc: The union of the causal past and future of a set.
declarations.statement: def causalHull (A : Set M) : Set M

declarations.statement: lemma subset_causalFuture : A ⊆ C.causalFuture A

declarations.name: CausalRelation.subset_causalPast
declarations.statement: lemma subset_causalPast : A ⊆ C.causalPast A

declarations.name: CausalRelation.causalFuture_mono
declarations.statement: lemma causalFuture_mono (h : A ⊆ B) : C.causalFuture A ⊆ C.causalFuture B

declarations.name: CausalRelation.causalPast_mono

declarations.name: CausalRelation.causalHull_mono
declarations.statement: lemma causalHull_mono (h : A ⊆ B) : C.causalHull A ⊆ C.causalHull B

declarations.name: CausalRelation.causalFuture_empty
declarations.statement: lemma causalFuture_empty : C.causalFuture ∅ = ∅

declarations.name: CausalRelation.causalPast_empty
declarations.statement: lemma causalPast_empty : C.causalPast ∅ = ∅

declarations.name: CausalRelation.causalFuture_union

declarations.name: CausalRelation.causalPast_union

declarations.name: CausalRelation.IsSpacelikeCompact
declarations.doc:
A closed field support is spacelike compact when it lies in the causal hull of a compact set.
No equivalence with a Cauchy-surface definition is asserted without geometric hypotheses.
declarations.statement: def IsSpacelikeCompact [TopologicalSpace M] (A : Set M) : Prop

declarations.name: CausalRelation.IsSpacelikeCompact.mono
declarations.statement:
lemma IsSpacelikeCompact.mono [TopologicalSpace M]
    (hB : C.IsSpacelikeCompact B) (h : A ⊆ B) : C.IsSpacelikeCompact A

declarations.name: CausalRelation.HasCompactCausalDiamonds
declarations.doc:
Compact causal diamonds are the geometric compactness input for Green exactness.
This does not by itself assert every part of global hyperbolicity.
declarations.statement: def HasCompactCausalDiamonds [TopologicalSpace M] : Prop

declarations.name: CausalRelation.HasCompactCausalDiamonds.reverse
declarations.doc: Compact causal diamonds are unchanged by reversing time orientation.
declarations.statement:
lemma HasCompactCausalDiamonds.reverse [TopologicalSpace M]
    (h : C.HasCompactCausalDiamonds) : C.reverse.HasCompactCausalDiamonds

declarations.name: CausalRelation.IsPastCompact
declarations.doc:
A set is past compact when its intersection with the causal past of every compact set is
compact.
declarations.statement: def IsPastCompact (A : Set M) : Prop

declarations.name: CausalRelation.isPastCompact_empty
declarations.statement: lemma isPastCompact_empty : C.IsPastCompact ∅

declarations.name: CausalRelation.IsPastCompact.union
declarations.statement:
lemma IsPastCompact.union (hA : C.IsPastCompact A) (hB : C.IsPastCompact B) :
    C.IsPastCompact (A ∪ B)

declarations.name: CausalRelation.IsPastCompact.mono
declarations.doc: A closed subset of a past-compact set remains past compact.
declarations.statement:
lemma IsPastCompact.mono (hB : C.IsPastCompact B) (hA : IsClosed A) (hAB : A ⊆ B) :
    C.IsPastCompact A

declarations.name: CausalRelation.causalFuture_inter_causalPast
declarations.doc: Causal transitivity localizes a future inside the past of an observation set.
declarations.statement:
lemma causalFuture_inter_causalPast (A K : Set M) :
    C.causalFuture A ∩ C.causalPast K =

modules.title: Step approximation in vector lattices
modules.doc:
Freudenthal's spectral theorem: vector lattice elements are uniformly close to step functions.

## i. Overview

Fix a nonnegative element `u` of a real vector lattice, a strong unit: every element is below some
multiple of `u`. Every element is then close to a step function: split `u` into finitely many
disjoint pieces, and on each piece replace the element by a constant multiple of the piece. The
pieces form a partition of `u`: nonnegative, pairwise disjoint, adding up to `u`.

Finding the pieces needs least upper bounds of increasing sequences below `u`. Given `y`, the
increasing sequence `n • y⁺ ⊓ u` approaches the part of `u` on which `y` is positive: its support.
For an element `x` and a level `a`, the support of `x - a • u` is the piece on which `x` exceeds
`a`.
Cutting `u` at finitely many levels produces a partition on whose pieces `x` varies by at most the
spacing of the levels. Several elements are handled by intersecting their partitions.

## ii. Key results

- `VectorLattice.IsPartition` : a partition of `u`.
- `VectorLattice.IsPartition.le_sum` : local upper bounds on the pieces of a partition give a
  global upper bound.
- `VectorLattice.support_inf_sub` : the support of an element is a component of `u`.
- `VectorLattice.exists_partition_approx` : finitely many elements are uniformly close to step
  functions on one common partition. This is Freudenthal's spectral theorem.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Partitions
- B. Step functions
- C. From local to global bounds
- D. Supports
- E. Partitions along one element
- F. Common refinements
- G. Components below a multiple of the unit

## iv. References

- W. A. J. Luxemburg and A. C. Zaanen, *Riesz Spaces I*, North-Holland, 1971, §40.

sections.text: ## C. From local to global bounds

declarations.name: VectorLattice.inf_eq_zero_of_le
declarations.doc: Disjointness passes to smaller nonnegative elements.
declarations.statement:
lemma inf_eq_zero_of_le {w v v' : G} (hw : 0 ≤ w) (hv : 0 ≤ v) (hvv : v ≤ v') (h : w ⊓ v' = 0) :
    w ⊓ v = 0

declarations.name: VectorLattice.IsPartition
declarations.doc: A partition of `u`: nonnegative, pairwise disjoint pieces that add up to `u`.
declarations.statement: def IsPartition {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] (s : ι → G) : Prop

declarations.name: VectorLattice.IsPartition.inf_sum_erase
declarations.doc: The pieces of a partition other than `i` add up to an element disjoint from `s i`.
declarations.statement:
lemma IsPartition.inf_sum_erase [DecidableEq ι] (hs : IsPartition u s) (i : ι) :
    s i ⊓ ∑ j ∈ Finset.univ.erase i, s j = 0

declarations.name: VectorLattice.IsPartition.le
declarations.statement: lemma IsPartition.le (hs : IsPartition u s) (i : ι) : s i ≤ u

declarations.name: VectorLattice.IsPartition.inf_sub
declarations.doc: A piece of a partition is disjoint from its complement.
declarations.statement: lemma IsPartition.inf_sub [DecidableEq ι] (hs : IsPartition u s) (i : ι) : s i ⊓ (u - s i) = 0

declarations.name: VectorLattice.isPartition_sub_succ
declarations.doc: Differences of an antitone sequence of components from `u` to `0` form a partition.
declarations.statement:
lemma isPartition_sub_succ {N : ℕ} {e : ℕ → G} (he : Antitone e) (h0 : e 0 = u) (hN : e N = 0)
    (hnn : ∀ j, 0 ≤ e j) (hle : ∀ j, e j ≤ u) (hc : ∀ j, e j ⊓ (u - e j) = 0) :
    IsPartition u fun j : Fin N => e j - e (j + 1)

declarations.name: VectorLattice.IsPartition.inf_prod
declarations.doc: The pairwise infima of two partitions form a partition.
declarations.statement:
lemma IsPartition.inf_prod (hs : IsPartition u s) {κ : Type*} [Fintype κ] {t : κ → G}
    (ht : IsPartition u t) : IsPartition u fun p : ι × κ => s p.1 ⊓ t p.2

declarations.name: VectorLattice.IsPartition.comp_equiv
declarations.statement:
lemma IsPartition.comp_equiv (hs : IsPartition u s) {κ : Type*} [Fintype κ] (e : κ ≃ ι) :
    IsPartition u (s ∘ e)

declarations.name: VectorLattice.IsPartition.inf_smul
declarations.doc: A nonnegative element splits along a partition: `x ⊓ M • u` is the sum of `x ⊓ M • s i`.
declarations.statement:
lemma IsPartition.inf_smul (hs : IsPartition u s) {x : G} (hx : 0 ≤ x) {M : ℝ} (hM : 0 ≤ M) :
    x ⊓ M • u = ∑ i, x ⊓ M • s i

declarations.name: VectorLattice.IsPartition.sum_smul_le
declarations.doc: A step function whose levels on the nonzero pieces are at most `ε` is at most `ε • u`.
declarations.statement:
lemma IsPartition.sum_smul_le (hs : IsPartition u s) {c : ι → ℝ} {ε : ℝ}
    (h : ∀ i, s i ≠ 0 → c i ≤ ε) : ∑ i, c i • s i ≤ ε • u

declarations.name: VectorLattice.IsPartition.le_sum_smul
declarations.doc: A step function whose levels on the nonzero pieces are at least `ε` is at least `ε • u`.
declarations.statement:
lemma IsPartition.le_sum_smul (hs : IsPartition u s) {c : ι → ℝ} {ε : ℝ}
    (h : ∀ i, s i ≠ 0 → ε ≤ c i) : ε • u ≤ ∑ i, c i • s i

declarations.name: VectorLattice.IsPartition.sub_sum_le
declarations.doc:
Away from the piece `s i`, a step function differs from its level on `s i` by at most the
spacing of the levels.
declarations.statement:
lemma IsPartition.sub_sum_le (x : G) (b : ι → ℝ) (i : ι) :
    x - ∑ j, b j • s j ≤ (x - b i • u)⁺ + ∑ j ∈ Finset.univ.erase i, |b i - b j| • s j

declarations.name: VectorLattice.IsPartition.sum_erase_inf_smul
declarations.doc: The other pieces of a partition, scaled, are disjoint from a scaled piece.
declarations.statement:
lemma IsPartition.sum_erase_inf_smul {c : ι → ℝ} (hc : ∀ j, 0 ≤ c j) (i : ι) {M : ℝ}
    (hM : 0 ≤ M) : (∑ j ∈ Finset.univ.erase i, c j • s j) ⊓ M • s i = 0

declarations.name: VectorLattice.IsPartition.posPart_sub_sum_inf
declarations.doc:
If `x` is at most `b i` on each piece, the excess of `x` over the step function vanishes on
each piece.
declarations.statement:
lemma IsPartition.posPart_sub_sum_inf {x : G} {b : ι → ℝ} (h : ∀ i, (x - b i • u)⁺ ⊓ s i = 0)
    (i : ι) {M : ℝ} (hM : 0 ≤ M) : (x - ∑ j, b j • s j)⁺ ⊓ M • s i = 0

declarations.name: VectorLattice.IsPartition.le_sum
declarations.doc:
**Local to global.** If on each piece `s i` of a partition the element `x` is at most `b i`,
then `x` is at most the step function `∑ b i • s i`.
declarations.statement:
lemma IsPartition.le_sum (hunit : IsStrongUnit u) {x : G} {b : ι → ℝ}
    (h : ∀ i, (x - b i • u)⁺ ⊓ s i = 0) : x ≤ ∑ i, b i • s i

declarations.name: VectorLattice.IsPartition.sum_le
declarations.doc:
**Local to global, from below.** If on each piece `s i` of a partition the element `x` is at
least `a i`, then `x` is at least the step function `∑ a i • s i`.
declarations.statement:
lemma IsPartition.sum_le (hunit : IsStrongUnit u) {x : G} {a : ι → ℝ}
    (h : ∀ i, (a i • u - x)⁺ ⊓ s i = 0) : ∑ i, a i • s i ≤ x

declarations.name: VectorLattice.HasMonotoneSups
declarations.doc: Increasing sequences below `u` have least upper bounds.
declarations.statement: def HasMonotoneSups : Prop

declarations.name: VectorLattice.monotone_smul_posPart_inf
declarations.statement: lemma monotone_smul_posPart_inf (y : G) : Monotone fun n : ℕ => (n : ℝ) • y⁺ ⊓ u

declarations.name: VectorLattice.exists_isLUB_support
declarations.statement:
lemma exists_isLUB_support (y : G) :
    ∃ c, IsLUB (Set.range fun n : ℕ => (n : ℝ) • y⁺ ⊓ u) c

declarations.name: VectorLattice.support
declarations.doc: The support of `y`: the part of `u` on which `y` is positive, the limit of `n • y⁺ ⊓ u`.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def support (y : G) : G

declarations.name: VectorLattice.isLUB_support
declarations.statement:
lemma isLUB_support (y : G) :
    IsLUB (Set.range fun n : ℕ => (n : ℝ) • y⁺ ⊓ u) (support hsup y)

declarations.name: VectorLattice.le_support
declarations.statement: lemma le_support (y : G) (n : ℕ) : (n : ℝ) • y⁺ ⊓ u ≤ support hsup y

declarations.name: VectorLattice.support_le
declarations.statement: lemma support_le (y : G) : support hsup y ≤ u

declarations.name: VectorLattice.support_mono
declarations.statement: lemma support_mono {y y' : G} (h : y ≤ y') : support hsup y ≤ support hsup y'

declarations.name: VectorLattice.support_nonneg
declarations.statement: lemma support_nonneg (y : G) : 0 ≤ support hsup y

declarations.name: VectorLattice.support_inf_sub
declarations.doc: The support is a component of `u`: it is disjoint from its complement.
declarations.statement: lemma support_inf_sub (y : G) : support hsup y ⊓ (u - support hsup y) = 0

declarations.name: VectorLattice.inf_support_eq_zero
declarations.doc: A nonnegative element disjoint from `y⁺` is disjoint from the support of `y`.
declarations.statement: lemma inf_support_eq_zero {w y : G} (hw : 0 ≤ w) (h : w ⊓ y⁺ = 0) : w ⊓ support hsup y = 0

declarations.name: VectorLattice.posPart_inf_sub_support
declarations.doc: `y⁺` lives on the support of `y`: it is disjoint from the complement.
declarations.statement: lemma posPart_inf_sub_support (y : G) : y⁺ ⊓ (u - support hsup y) = 0

declarations.name: VectorLattice.support_eq_zero
declarations.statement: lemma support_eq_zero {y : G} (hy : y ≤ 0) : support hsup y = 0

declarations.name: VectorLattice.support_eq_self
declarations.statement: lemma support_eq_self {y : G} (hy : u ≤ y) : support hsup y = u

declarations.name: VectorLattice.posPart_sub_inf_support
declarations.doc:
Where `x` exceeds `a`, it is at least `a`: `(a • u - x)⁺` is disjoint from the support of
`x - a • u`.
declarations.statement:
lemma posPart_sub_inf_support (x : G) (a : ℝ) :
    (a • u - x)⁺ ⊓ support hsup (x - a • u) = 0

declarations.name: VectorLattice.levelSupport
declarations.doc: The support of `x - (L + j * δ) • u`: the piece of `u` on which `x` exceeds the `j`-th level.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def levelSupport (L δ : ℝ) (j : ℕ) : G

declarations.name: VectorLattice.levelSupport_antitone
declarations.statement: lemma levelSupport_antitone : Antitone (levelSupport hsup x L δ)

declarations.name: VectorLattice.isPartition_levelSupport
declarations.doc:
Cutting `u` at the levels `L + j * δ` gives a partition once the levels pass below and above
`x`.
declarations.statement:
lemma isPartition_levelSupport {N : ℕ} (h0 : u ≤ x - L • u) (hN : x ≤ (L + N * δ) • u) :
    IsPartition u fun j : Fin N => levelSupport hsup x L δ j - levelSupport hsup x L δ (j + 1)

declarations.name: VectorLattice.levelSupport_approx
declarations.doc: On the `j`-th piece, `x` lies between the `j`-th and the `(j + 1)`-th level.
declarations.statement:
lemma levelSupport_approx (j : ℕ) :
    (x - (L + j * δ + δ) • u)⁺ ⊓ (levelSupport hsup x L δ j - levelSupport hsup x L δ (j + 1)) = 0
      ∧ ((L + j * δ) • u - x)⁺ ⊓
        (levelSupport hsup x L δ j - levelSupport hsup x L δ (j + 1)) = 0

declarations.name: VectorLattice.exists_partition_approx_one
declarations.doc: One element is within `δ` of a step function: cut `u` at levels spaced by `δ`.
declarations.statement:
lemma exists_partition_approx_one (hsup : HasMonotoneSups u) (hu : 0 ≤ u)
    (hunit : IsStrongUnit u) (x : G) {δ : ℝ} (hδ : 0 < δ) :
    ∃ (N : ℕ) (s : Fin N → G) (a : Fin N → ℝ), IsPartition u s ∧
      ∀ j, (x - (a j + δ) • u)⁺ ⊓ s j = 0 ∧ (a j • u - x)⁺ ⊓ s j = 0

declarations.name: VectorLattice.approx_of_le
declarations.doc: Bounds on the pieces of a partition hold on the pieces of every refinement.
declarations.statement:
lemma approx_of_le {x c c' : G} {a δ : ℝ} (hc : 0 ≤ c) (hcc : c ≤ c')
    (h : (x - (a + δ) • u)⁺ ⊓ c' = 0 ∧ (a • u - x)⁺ ⊓ c' = 0) :
    (x - (a + δ) • u)⁺ ⊓ c = 0 ∧ (a • u - x)⁺ ⊓ c = 0

declarations.name: VectorLattice.exists_partition_approx
declarations.doc:
**Freudenthal's spectral theorem.** Finitely many elements are within `δ` of step functions on
one common partition of `u`.
declarations.statement:
lemma exists_partition_approx (hsup : HasMonotoneSups u) (hu : 0 ≤ u) (hunit : IsStrongUnit u)
    {n : ℕ} (x : Fin n → G) {δ : ℝ} (hδ : 0 < δ) :
    ∃ (m : ℕ) (s : Fin m → G) (a : Fin m → Fin n → ℝ), IsPartition u s ∧
      ∀ i k, (x k - (a i k + δ) • u)⁺ ⊓ s i = 0 ∧ (a i k • u - x k)⁺ ⊓ s i = 0

declarations.name: VectorLattice.eq_zero_of_le_smul
declarations.doc: A component of `u` that is strictly below `u` in the sense `c ≤ t • u`, `t < 1`, vanishes.
declarations.statement:
lemma eq_zero_of_le_smul (hu : 0 ≤ u) {c : G} (hc0 : 0 ≤ c) (hc : c ⊓ (u - c) = 0) {t : ℝ}
    (ht : t < 1) (h : c ≤ t • u) : c = 0

modules.title: Positive functionals
modules.doc:
Positive functionals on an ordered vector space, their order, and extension from the cone.

## i. Overview

A positive functional on an ordered real vector space `E` is a linear functional that is
nonnegative on the positive cone. When the order is directed, every element is a difference of
two nonnegative ones, so positive functionals are determined by their values on the cone. They are
then ordered by comparing these values: `ψ ≤ φ` when `φ - ψ` is positive again.

Conversely, a nonnegative function on the cone that is additive and positively homogeneous there
extends uniquely to a positive functional.

## ii. Key results

- `PositiveLinearMap.instPartialOrder` : positive functionals ordered on the positive cone.
- `PositiveLinearMap.subOfLE` : the difference of two positive functionals, one below the other.
- `PositiveLinearMap.eq_zero_of_map_eq_zero` : a positive functional vanishing at an order unit
  vanishes.
- `PositiveLinearMap.ofCone` : a nonnegative, additive, positively homogeneous function on the
  cone as a positive functional.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Scaling positive functionals
- B. The order on positive functionals
- C. Extending from the cone

## iv. References

* None.

modules.title: The bidual
modules.doc:
The bidual of an ordered vector space via positive functionals, and its monotone completeness.

## i. Overview

An element of an ordered real vector space `E` assigns to every positive functional its value,
additively and positively homogeneously, and dominated by the values of some element of `E`. The
bidual consists of all such assignments. It contains `E` when the order is directed, and is
ordered by comparing values on every positive functional. Positive functionals extend to the
bidual by evaluation.

The bidual is monotone complete: a bounded upward directed family of elements has a least upper
bound, their pointwise supremum.

## ii. Key results

- `Bidual E` : the bidual of `E`.
- `Bidual.ofE` : an element of `E` as an element of the bidual.
- `Bidual.eval` : a positive functional extended to the bidual.
- `Bidual.isLUB_ciSup` : a bounded directed family in the bidual has its pointwise supremum as
  least upper bound.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. The bidual
- B. Order
- C. Elements and positive functionals
- D. Monotone completeness

## iv. References

* None.

modules.title: The bidual as a lattice
modules.doc:
Least upper bounds in the bidual by the Riesz–Kantorovich formula; the bidual is a lattice.

## i. Overview

When the positive functionals on `E` form a lattice, any two elements `x` and `y` of the bidual have
a least upper bound. Its value on a positive functional `φ` is the best split of `φ` between `x`
and `y`: the supremum of `x φ₁ + y φ₂` over `φ = φ₁ + φ₂`. This is the Riesz–Kantorovich formula
with the roles of elements and functionals exchanged. The bidual then is a lattice.

## ii. Key results

- `Bidual.dsup` : the least upper bound of two elements of the bidual.
- `Bidual.isLUB_dsup` : it is the least upper bound.
- `Bidual.instLattice` : when the positive functionals form a lattice, the bidual is a lattice.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Best splits of a positive functional
- B. The least upper bound
- C. The lattice structure

## iv. References

* None.

modules.title: Approximate interpolation
modules.doc:
Approximate interpolation between finite families when the positive functionals form a lattice.

## i. Overview

Given finitely many lower elements `a i` below finitely many upper elements `b j` of an ordered
real vector space with an order unit `u`, an interpolant is an element `g` with `a i ≤ g ≤ b j` for
all `i` and `j`. When the positive functionals form a lattice, interpolants exist up to any error:
for every `ε > 0` some `g` has `a i ≤ g + ε • u` and `g ≤ b j + ε • u`. The proof measures the
failure to interpolate by a sublinear gauge; Hahn–Banach turns a linear functional below it into
positive functionals, and refining these in the lattice of positive functionals shows the gauge is
not positive.

## ii. Key results

- `HasLatticeDualCone.exists_table` : two finite families of positive functionals with the same sum
  have a common refinement.
- `Interpolation.gauge` : the interpolation gauge.
- `Interpolation.exists_linear_le_gauge` : a linear functional below the interpolation gauge.
- `HasLatticeDualCone.exists_approx_interpolant` : approximate interpolants exist.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Refinement tables
- B. The interpolation gauge
- C. Approximate interpolants

## iv. References

* None.

declarations.name: HasLatticeDualCone.exists_table
declarations.doc:
Two finite families of positive functionals with the same sum have a common refinement: a table
whose rows add up to the first family and whose columns add up to the second.
declarations.statement:
lemma exists_table {n : ℕ} (θ : Fin n → E →ₚ[ℝ] ℝ) : ∀ {m : ℕ} (θ' : Fin m → E →ₚ[ℝ] ℝ),
    ∑ i, θ i = ∑ j, θ' j → ∃ τ : Fin n → Fin m → E →ₚ[ℝ] ℝ,
      (∀ i, ∑ j, τ i j = θ i) ∧ ∀ j, ∑ i, τ i j = θ' j
  | 0, θ', h => ⟨fun _ j => j.elim0, fun i => by
      simp only [Finset.univ_eq_empty, Finset.sum_empty] at h ⊢
      exact (le_antisymm (h ▸ le_sum θ (Finset.mem_univ i)) (zero_le _)).symm,
      fun j => j.elim0⟩
  | m + 1, θ', h => by
    rw [Fin.sum_univ_succ] at h
    obtain ⟨ψ₁, ψ₂, hψ, s₁, s₂⟩

modules.title: Positive majorants
modules.doc:
A positive functional of weight at most m at u that dominates P - N, via Hahn–Banach.

## i. Overview

Fix an order unit `u` and two positive functionals `P` and `N`. If `P - N` is at most
`m` on the order interval `[0, u]`, then `P` lies below `π + N` for a positive functional `π` with
`π u ≤ m`. The functional `π` comes from Hahn–Banach, applied to a gauge that measures how much
`P - N` can exceed `m` times the multiple of `u` needed to dominate an element.

## ii. Key results

- `PositiveLinearMap.majorant` : the majorant gauge.
- `PositiveLinearMap.exists_le_add_of_forall_le` : a positive functional of weight at most `m` at
  `u` that makes up for `P - N`.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. The majorant gauge
- B. Positive majorants

## iv. References

* None.

modules.title: The Riesz–Kantorovich formula
modules.doc:
Riesz decomposition makes positive functionals a lattice via the Riesz–Kantorovich formula.

## i. Overview

An ordered real vector space has the Riesz decomposition when a nonnegative element below a sum of
two nonnegative elements splits into pieces below the summands. Vector lattices have it. Then any
two positive functionals have a least upper bound, given by the Riesz–Kantorovich formula
`(φ ⊔ ψ) f = sup {φ g + ψ (f - g) | 0 ≤ g ≤ f}`: the positive functionals form a lattice.

In a lattice of positive functionals, a positive functional below a sum splits into pieces below
the summands, and finite families with the same sum have common refinements.

## ii. Key results

- `HasRieszDecomposition E` : the Riesz decomposition.
- `PositiveLinearMap.isLUB_rkSup` : the Riesz–Kantorovich formula gives the least upper bound.
- `HasLatticeDualCone E` : the positive functionals form a lattice.
- `HasRieszDecomposition.hasLatticeDualCone` : the Riesz decomposition makes the positive
  functionals a lattice.
- `VectorLattice.hasLatticeDualCone` : the positive functionals on a vector lattice form a lattice.
- `HasLatticeDualCone.exists_refinement` : positive functionals refine.
- `PositiveLinearMap.HasRefinement` : finite families with the same sum have a common refinement.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. The Riesz–Kantorovich supremum
- B. The lattice dual cone
- C. Riesz decomposition of positive functionals
- D. Finite refinement of positive functionals

## iv. References

- C. D. Aliprantis and O. Burkinshaw, *Positive Operators*, Springer, 2006, ch. 1.
- E. M. Alfsen, *Compact Convex Sets and Boundary Integrals*, Springer, 1971, ch. II.

modules.title: Upper envelopes
modules.doc:
Splittings of a positive functional attain the upper envelope of a finite family.

## i. Overview

Take finitely many elements `A₁, …, Aₙ` of a directed ordered real vector space and a positive
functional `φ`. Their upper envelope at `φ` is the smallest value `φ B` over all common upper
bounds `B` of the `Aᵢ`.

Split `φ` into positive pieces `φ₁ + … + φₙ` and let each piece evaluate its own element. The
total `φ₁ A₁ + … + φₙ Aₙ` never exceeds the upper envelope, and by the Hahn–Banach theorem some
splitting reaches it.

## ii. Key results

- `PositiveLinearMap.upperEnvelope` is the upper envelope of finitely many elements.
- `PositiveLinearMap.sum_apply_le_upperEnvelope` proves that splittings stay below the upper
  envelope.
- `PositiveLinearMap.exists_sum_eq_upperEnvelope` proves that some splitting reaches it.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Upper envelopes
- B. Splittings attain the upper envelope

## iv. References

- E. M. Alfsen, *Compact Convex Sets and Boundary Integrals*, Springer, 1971, ch. I.3, II.3.

Splitting a functional and letting each piece evaluate its own element stays below the

declarations.doc: **Duality**: some splitting of the functional attains the upper envelope.

modules.title: Strong units
modules.doc:
Strong units and order units of ordered abelian groups, and the directed order they induce.

## i. Overview

A strong unit of an ordered abelian group is an element `u` such that every element lies below some
natural multiple of `u`; an order unit is a nonnegative strong unit. A group with a nonnegative
strong unit is directed: any two elements lie below a common multiple of `u`. In a nontrivial
group a strong unit is nonzero.

## ii. Key results

- `IsStrongUnit` : every element lies below a natural multiple of `u`.
- `IsStrongUnit.exists_two_sided` : every element lies between opposite multiples of `u`.
- `IsStrongUnit.isDirectedOrder` : a nonnegative strong unit makes the order directed.
- `IsStrongUnit.ne_zero` : a strong unit of a nontrivial group is nonzero.
- `IsOrderUnit` : a nonnegative strong unit.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Strong units
- B. Order units

## iv. References

* None.

declarations.name: IsStrongUnit
declarations.doc: A strong unit: every element lies below some natural multiple of `u`.
declarations.statement: def IsStrongUnit : Prop

declarations.name: IsStrongUnit.exists_two_sided
declarations.doc: Every element lies between two opposite multiples of a nonnegative strong unit.
declarations.statement:
lemma exists_two_sided (hunit : IsStrongUnit u) (hu : 0 ≤ u) (x : G) :

  /-- An order unit is nonnegative. -/

    ∃ μ : ℝ, 0 ≤ μ ∧ ∀ i, x i ≤ μ • u

modules.title: Vector lattices
modules.doc:
Elementary arithmetic of infima in real vector lattices: Riesz decomposition and disjointness.

## i. Overview

A real vector lattice is an ordered real vector space in which any two elements have a least upper
bound. Two nonnegative elements are disjoint when their infimum is `0`. This file collects the
elementary arithmetic of infima: the Riesz decomposition, the behaviour of infima under positive
scalars, and how disjointness interacts with sums and with least upper bounds of sequences.

## ii. Key results

- `VectorLattice.riesz_decomposition` : an element below a sum of two nonnegative elements splits
  into two pieces, one below each summand.
- `VectorLattice.smul_inf` : positive scalars distribute over infima.
- `VectorLattice.inf_sum_of_pairwise` : infima distribute over sums of pairwise disjoint nonnegative
  elements.
- `VectorLattice.isLUB_inf` : infima distribute over least upper bounds of sequences.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Riesz decomposition and disjointness
- B. Positive scalars

## iv. References

* None.

declarations.name: VectorLattice.posPart_le_of_le
declarations.doc: The positive part of an element below a nonnegative element is below it.
declarations.statement: lemma posPart_le_of_le {y z : G} (h : y ≤ z) (hz : 0 ≤ z) : y⁺ ≤ z

declarations.name: VectorLattice.riesz_decomposition
declarations.doc:
**Riesz decomposition**: if `0 ≤ g ≤ f₁ + f₂` with `0 ≤ f₁, f₂`, then `g ⊓ f₁` and
`g - g ⊓ f₁` split `g` into pieces between `0` and `f₁`, resp. `f₂`.
declarations.statement:
lemma riesz_decomposition {f₁ f₂ g : G} (h₁ : 0 ≤ f₁) (h₂ : 0 ≤ f₂) (hg0 : 0 ≤ g)
    (hg : g ≤ f₁ + f₂) :
    0 ≤ g ⊓ f₁ ∧ g ⊓ f₁ ≤ f₁ ∧ 0 ≤ g - g ⊓ f₁ ∧ g - g ⊓ f₁ ≤ f₂

declarations.name: VectorLattice.add_inf_le
declarations.doc:
The infimum of a sum of nonnegative elements with a nonnegative element is at most the sum of
the infima.
declarations.statement:
lemma add_inf_le {h₁ h₂ c : G} (h₁0 : 0 ≤ h₁) (h₂0 : 0 ≤ h₂) (hc : 0 ≤ c) :
    (h₁ + h₂) ⊓ c ≤ h₁ ⊓ c + h₂ ⊓ c

declarations.name: VectorLattice.inf_add_of_inf_eq_zero
declarations.doc: Disjoint nonnegative elements split every nonnegative element additively.
declarations.statement:
lemma inf_add_of_inf_eq_zero {x u v : G} (hx : 0 ≤ x) (hu : 0 ≤ u) (hv : 0 ≤ v) (h : u ⊓ v = 0) :
    x ⊓ (u + v) = x ⊓ u + x ⊓ v

declarations.name: VectorLattice.inf_add_eq_zero
declarations.doc: An element disjoint from two nonnegative elements is disjoint from their sum.
declarations.statement:
lemma inf_add_eq_zero {x u v : G} (hx : 0 ≤ x) (hu : 0 ≤ u) (hv : 0 ≤ v) (hxu : x ⊓ u = 0)
    (hxv : x ⊓ v = 0) : x ⊓ (u + v) = 0

declarations.name: VectorLattice.inf_sum_eq_zero
declarations.doc:
An element disjoint from every member of a finite family of nonnegative elements is disjoint
from their sum.
declarations.statement:
lemma inf_sum_eq_zero {ι : Type*} (s : Finset ι) {x : G} (hx : 0 ≤ x) (u : ι → G)
    (hu : ∀ i ∈ s, 0 ≤ u i) (h : ∀ i ∈ s, x ⊓ u i = 0) : x ⊓ ∑ i ∈ s, u i = 0

declarations.name: VectorLattice.add_inf_le_of_inf_eq_zero
declarations.doc:
A nonnegative element below `x + w`, where `w` is disjoint from `s`, meets `s` at most where
`x` does.
declarations.statement:
lemma add_inf_le_of_inf_eq_zero {x w s : G} (hx : 0 ≤ x) (hw : 0 ≤ w) (hs : 0 ≤ s)
    (h : w ⊓ s = 0) : (x + w) ⊓ s ≤ x ⊓ s

declarations.name: VectorLattice.inf_sum_of_pairwise
declarations.doc:
A nonnegative element splits along a finite family of pairwise disjoint nonnegative
elements.
declarations.statement:
lemma inf_sum_of_pairwise {κ : Type*} (t : Finset κ) {x : G} (hx : 0 ≤ x) (u : κ → G)
    (hu : ∀ i ∈ t, 0 ≤ u i) (hd : ∀ i ∈ t, ∀ j ∈ t, i ≠ j → u i ⊓ u j = 0) :
    x ⊓ ∑ i ∈ t, u i = ∑ i ∈ t, x ⊓ u i

declarations.name: VectorLattice.isLUB_inf
declarations.doc: Infima distribute over least upper bounds of sequences.
declarations.statement:
lemma isLUB_inf {a : ℕ → G} {c : G} (ha : IsLUB (Set.range a) c) (b : G) :
    IsLUB (Set.range fun n => a n ⊓ b) (c ⊓ b)

declarations.name: VectorLattice.smul_inf
declarations.doc: Positive scalars distribute over infima.
declarations.statement: lemma smul_inf {c : ℝ} (hc : 0 ≤ c) (x y : G) : c • (x ⊓ y) = c • x ⊓ c • y

declarations.name: VectorLattice.inf_smul_eq_zero
declarations.doc: Disjoint nonnegative elements stay disjoint after scaling one of them.
declarations.statement:
lemma inf_smul_eq_zero {g u : G} (hg : 0 ≤ g) (hu : 0 ≤ u) (h : g ⊓ u = 0) {a : ℝ} (ha : 0 ≤ a) :
    g ⊓ a • u = 0

declarations.name: VectorLattice.smul_inf_smul_eq_zero
declarations.doc: Disjoint nonnegative elements stay disjoint after scaling both.
declarations.statement:
lemma smul_inf_smul_eq_zero {u v : G} (hu : 0 ≤ u) (hv : 0 ≤ v) (h : u ⊓ v = 0) {a b : ℝ}
    (ha : 0 ≤ a) (hb : 0 ≤ b) : a • u ⊓ b • v = 0

declarations.name: VectorLattice.isLUB_smul
declarations.doc: Positive scalars preserve least upper bounds of sequences.
declarations.statement:
lemma isLUB_smul {a : ℕ → G} {c : G} (ha : IsLUB (Set.range a) c) {r : ℝ} (hr : 0 < r) :
    IsLUB (Set.range fun n => r • a n) (r • c)

modules.title: The Second Partial Derivatives Test
modules.doc:
A positive definite Hessian at a critical point of an analytic function gives a local minimum.

## i. Overview

We prove a version of the second partial derivative test from calculus for
analytic functions `f : V → ℝ`, where `V` is a finite-dimensional vector space.

The second iterated Fréchet derivative is packaged as a quadratic map, a positive definite
quadratic map is shown to be coercive, and a little-o form of the test is combined with the
quadratic approximation coming from a power series.

Tags: partial derivative test, calculus.

## ii. Key results

- `iteratedFDerivQuadraticMap` : the second iterated Fréchet derivative as a quadratic map.
- `coercive_of_posdef` : positive definiteness implies coercivity.
- `isLocalMin_of_posDef_of_littleo` : the second partial derivative test, "little oh" form.
- `second_derivative_test` : Suppose `f` is a real-valued function on a finite-dimensional inner
  product space that has vanishing gradient at `x₀`, and has a power series on a ball of positive
  radius around `x₀`. If the second Fréchet derivative is positive definite at `x₀` then `f` has a
  local minimum at `x₀`.
- `second_derivative_test_analyticAt` : the same test, assuming only that `f` is analytic at `x₀`.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Updating vectors of length two
- B. Quadratic maps from the second derivative
- C. Coercivity of positive definite forms
- D. The second derivative test

## iv. References

* None.

declarations.statement:
theorem le_of_littleO {V : Type*}
    [NormedAddCommGroup V] [InnerProductSpace ℝ V]
    {f : V → ℝ} {x₀ x : V} {C : ℝ}

modules.title: Polynomials with coefficients in an algebra
modules.doc:
## i. Overview

A polynomial whose coefficients lie in a `k`-algebra `A` can be evaluated at the image
`algebraMap k A c` of a scalar. This file records that such a polynomial is determined by
those evaluations alone, when `k` is an infinite field, and defines the polynomial obtained
by applying a `k`-linear map to every coefficient.

Both are used to transport grading statements between two equivalent descriptions of a
grading on a jet algebra: the *mass-weight polynomial*, whose `X ^ n` coefficient is the
weight-`n` part of an element, and the *mass-weight scaling*, the algebra map scaling each
weight-`n` part by `c ^ n`. The scaling is the evaluation of the polynomial, so a statement
about one transfers to the other.

The determinacy is not an instance of `Polynomial.funext`: the coefficient ring `A` is
neither commutative nor a domain in the intended applications. It holds because `A` is a
`k`-vector space, so its elements are separated by linear functionals, and a polynomial over
the infinite field `k` is determined by its values.

## ii. Key results

- `Polynomial.eq_zero_of_forall_eval_algebraMap_eq_zero` : a polynomial vanishing at every
  scalar is zero.
- `Polynomial.ext_of_forall_eval_algebraMap` : two polynomials agreeing at every scalar are
  equal.
- `Polynomial.mapCoeffs` : apply a linear map to every coefficient.
- `Polynomial.eval_algebraMap_mapCoeffs` : evaluation commutes with `mapCoeffs`.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Determinacy by evaluation at scalars
- B. Applying a linear map to the coefficients

## iv. References

* None.

sections.text: ## A. Determinacy by evaluation at scalars
## B. Applying a linear map to the coefficients

declarations.name: Polynomial.eq_zero_of_forall_eval_algebraMap_eq_zero
declarations.doc:
A polynomial with coefficients in an algebra over an infinite field vanishes as soon as
it vanishes at the image of every scalar. Linear functionals separate the coefficients,
and over an infinite field a polynomial is determined by its values.

declarations.name: Polynomial.ext_of_forall_eval_algebraMap
declarations.doc:
Two polynomials with coefficients in an algebra over an infinite field are equal as soon
as they agree at the image of every scalar.

declarations.name: Polynomial.mapCoeffs
declarations.doc:
The polynomial obtained by applying a function to every coefficient. Unlike
`Polynomial.map` this needs no multiplicativity, so it applies to derivations.

The argument is a bare function rather than a linear map: on an algebra built as a tensor
product the module structure coming from the algebra and the one coming from the tensor
product are equal but not syntactically so, and bundling would force the caller to
reconcile them. The properties needed are taken as hypotheses instead.
declarations.statement:
noncomputable def mapCoeffs {A : Type*} [Semiring A] (f : A → A) (p : Polynomial A) :
    Polynomial A

declarations.name: Polynomial.coeff_mapCoeffs
declarations.statement:
lemma coeff_mapCoeffs {A : Type*} [Semiring A] {f : A → A} (hf0 : f 0 = 0)
    (p : Polynomial A) (n : ℕ) : (mapCoeffs f p).coeff n = f (p.coeff n)

declarations.name: Polynomial.mapCoeffs_zero
declarations.statement: lemma mapCoeffs_zero {A : Type*} [Semiring A] (f : A → A) : mapCoeffs f 0 = 0

declarations.name: Polynomial.mapCoeffs_monomial
declarations.statement:
lemma mapCoeffs_monomial {A : Type*} [Semiring A] {f : A → A} (hf0 : f 0 = 0)
    (n : ℕ) (a : A) :
    mapCoeffs f (Polynomial.monomial n a) = Polynomial.monomial n (f a)

declarations.name: Polynomial.mapCoeffs_add
declarations.statement:
lemma mapCoeffs_add {A : Type*} [Semiring A] {f : A → A} (hf0 : f 0 = 0)
    (hadd : ∀ a b : A, f (a + b) = f a + f b) (p q : Polynomial A) :
    mapCoeffs f (p + q) = mapCoeffs f p + mapCoeffs f q

declarations.name: Polynomial.eval_algebraMap_mapAlgHom
declarations.doc:
Evaluation at a scalar commutes with pushing a polynomial along an algebra map: an
algebra map fixes the scalars.
declarations.statement:
lemma eval_algebraMap_mapAlgHom {k A B : Type*} [CommSemiring k] [Semiring A] [Semiring B]
    [Algebra k A] [Algebra k B] (f : A →ₐ[k] B) (p : Polynomial A) (c : k) :
    (Polynomial.mapAlgHom f p).eval (algebraMap k B c) = f (p.eval (algebraMap k A c))

declarations.name: Polynomial.eval_algebraMap_mapCoeffs
declarations.doc:
Evaluation at a scalar commutes with applying a linear map to the coefficients: the
powers of the scalar are central, so they pass through the linear map.
declarations.statement:
lemma eval_algebraMap_mapCoeffs {k A : Type*} [Field k] [Ring A] [Algebra k A]
    (f : A →ₗ[k] A) (p : Polynomial A) (c : k) :
    (mapCoeffs f p).eval (algebraMap k A c) = f (p.eval (algebraMap k A c))

declarations.name: Polynomial.eval_one_mapAlgHom
declarations.doc: Evaluation at one commutes with pushing a polynomial along an algebra map.
declarations.statement:
lemma eval_one_mapAlgHom {k A B : Type*} [CommSemiring k] [Semiring A] [Semiring B]
    [Algebra k A] [Algebra k B] (f : A →ₐ[k] B) (p : Polynomial A) :
    (Polynomial.mapAlgHom f p).eval 1 = f (p.eval 1)

declarations.name: Polynomial.mapCoeffs_mul_of_leibniz
declarations.doc:
A map satisfying the Leibniz rule satisfies it coefficientwise on polynomials. Applied to
a total derivative this is the Leibniz rule for the mass-weight polynomial.
declarations.statement:
lemma mapCoeffs_mul_of_leibniz {A : Type*} [Ring A] {D : A → A} (hD0 : D 0 = 0)
    (hDadd : ∀ a b : A, D (a + b) = D a + D b)
    (hD : ∀ a b : A, D (a * b) = D a * b + a * D b) (p q : Polynomial A) :
    mapCoeffs D (p * q) = mapCoeffs D p * q + p * mapCoeffs D q

modules.title: Factorization of Markov kernels
modules.doc:
Factoring kernels through Markov kernels, almost everywhere variants, and common refinements.

## i. Overview

A kernel `K : α → β` factors through a kernel `L : α → γ` when `K = κ ∘ₖ L` for some Markov kernel
`κ : γ → β`. Factoring through is a preorder on kernels with a common source; the target spaces
may differ. Relative to a measure `μ` on the source it suffices that the factorization holds at
`μ`-almost every point, and on a countably generated target, kernels that agree almost everywhere
on each measurable set agree almost everywhere. Two kernels have a common refinement when both
factor through a third one.

## ii. Key results

- `ProbabilityTheory.Kernel.FactorsThrough` : `K = κ ∘ₖ L` for a Markov kernel `κ`.
- `ProbabilityTheory.Kernel.MutuallyFactor` : factoring in both directions.
- `ProbabilityTheory.Kernel.FactorsThroughAE` : factoring at almost every point.
- `ProbabilityTheory.Kernel.ae_eq_of_forall_ae_apply_eq` : on a countably generated target,
  kernels that agree almost everywhere on each measurable set agree almost everywhere.
- `ProbabilityTheory.Kernel.HaveCommonRefinement` : both kernels factor through a third one.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Factorization
- B. Mutual factorization
- C. Factorization almost everywhere
- D. Mutual factorization almost everywhere
- E. Kernels equal almost everywhere
- F. Common refinements

## iv. References

* None.

modules.title: Dual representations on a dual basis
modules.doc:
## i. Overview

The dual of a representation acts on the dual basis by the transpose of the inverse: if
`ρ g⁻¹` has matrix `M` in a basis, then `ρ.dual g` sends each dual basis vector to the
combination given by the corresponding row of `M`.

## ii. Key results

- `Representation.dual_apply_dualBasis` : the dual representation on a dual basis.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. The dual representation on a dual basis

## iv. References

* None.

sections.text: ## A. The dual representation on a dual basis

declarations.name: Representation.dual_apply_dualBasis
declarations.doc:
The components of a dual representation on a dual basis: if `ρ g⁻¹` has
matrix `M` in the basis `b` (columns indexing the argument), then `ρ.dual g`
acts on the dual basis by the rows of `M`.
declarations.statement:
lemma dual_apply_dualBasis {k G V ι : Type*} [CommRing k]
    [Group G] [AddCommGroup V] [Module k V] [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    (ρ : Representation k G V) (b : Module.Basis ι k V) (g : G) (i : ι)
    (M : Matrix ι ι k) (hM : ∀ j, ρ g⁻¹ (b j) = ∑ l, M l j • b l) :
    ρ.dual g (b.dualBasis i) = ∑ j, M i j • b.dualBasis j

modules.title: The componentwise representation of a product group
modules.doc:
## i. Overview

Representations `ρ₁` of `G₁` on `V₁` and `ρ₂` of `G₂` on `V₂` give a representation of
`G₁ × G₂` on `V₁ × V₂`, acting componentwise. Mathlib's `Representation.prod` is the
diagonal action of a single group; this is the external product.

## ii. Key results

- `Representation.prodMap` : the componentwise representation.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. The componentwise representation

## iv. References

* None.

modules.title: The standard sl₂ Lie module
modules.doc:
Packages the standard module as a Lie module for the subalgebra generated by an `IsSl2Triple`.

## i. Overview

An `IsSl2Triple` generates a three-dimensional Lie subalgebra of endomorphisms. This file
uses the explicit standard-module operators to equip `StandardSl2Module` with a Lie module
structure for that subalgebra and records its action on coordinate vectors.

## ii. Key results

- `standardSl2ModuleLieRingModule` supplies the Lie module structure.
- Generator action lemmas give the raising, lowering, and weight formulas on the standard basis.
- `isSl2Triple_sub` packages the three generators as a triple inside their subalgebra.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. The generated Lie subalgebra
  - A.1. Public action formulas

## iv. References

- Mathlib, `Mathlib.Algebra.Lie.Sl2`.

## A. The generated Lie subalgebra

sections.text:
### A.1. Public action formulas

`standardSl2ModuleLieRingModule`'s bracket is built from `Construction.lean`'s `Φ`/
`ρE`/`ρF`/`ρH` machinery. The theorems below expose the action of `h`, `e`, `f` themselves on the
standard basis `v`, matching the formulas already recorded in `standardSl2ModuleLieRingModule`'s
own docstring, for downstream files (e.g. `Classification.lean`) that need to match a
module's own action against the standard one.

declarations.name: PhyslibAlpha.Sl2.Φ_leibniz
declarations.doc: The action map satisfies the Leibniz rule, since `Φ` preserves brackets.
declarations.statement:
lemma Φ_leibniz [CharZero K] (t : IsSl2Triple h e f) (x y : ↥(t.toLieSubalgebra (R := K)))
    (v : StandardSl2Module K n) :
    Φ (n := n) t x (Φ t y v) = Φ t ⁅x, y⁆ v + Φ t y (Φ t x v)

declarations.name: PhyslibAlpha.Sl2.standardSl2ModuleLieRingModule
declarations.doc:
Standard module `V(n)`, module structure.
Given an `sl₂`-triple `(h,e,f)` in `L`, `StandardSl2Module K n` carries a
`LieRingModule` structure for the generated subalgebra, with
`h ⬝ v k = (n - 2k) • v k`, `f ⬝ v k = v (k+1)` (and `f ⬝ v n = 0), and
`e ⬝ v k = (k * (n - k + 1)) • v (k-1)` (and `e ⬝ v 0 = 0`).
declarations.statement:
def standardSl2ModuleLieRingModule [CharZero K] (t : IsSl2Triple h e f) :
    LieRingModule (↥(t.toLieSubalgebra (R := K))) (StandardSl2Module K n)

declarations.name: PhyslibAlpha.Sl2.standardSl2ModuleLieModule
declarations.doc: Standard module `V(n)`, module structure, continued.
declarations.statement:
lemma standardSl2ModuleLieModule [CharZero K] (t : IsSl2Triple h e f) :
    letI := standardSl2ModuleLieRingModule (K := K) (n := n) t
    LieModule K ↥(t.toLieSubalgebra (R := K)) (StandardSl2Module K n)
